name: Iran
summary_text: Iran is among the most restrictive environments in the world for a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The Islamic Penal Code criminalises all same-sex activity for men and women, with penalties running from flogging to the death penalty, and the UK Home Office country report (CPIN, version 5.0, December 2025) records that the code carries no discrimination protections of any kind and that convictions are frequently brought on the pretext of more severe charges. Outright International confirms that same-sex relations are illegal nationwide for both sexes, and Human Rights Watch documented two men executed for homosexual conduct on 21 November 2005, the enforcement backdrop against which any visitor is assessed.  Recognition of trans status exists but is conditional. A 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini permits gender-reassignment surgery, which may be state-subsidised after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder", and Article 20, Clause 14 allows a person who has had sex reassignment surgery to change name and gender on the birth certificate by court order, with corrected identity documents reportedly issued efficiently and transparently. The Home Office report sets the limits: recognition follows only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process; the surgery available is invasive and often sub-standard; and an LGBT+ person living openly without recognised surgery is likely to face persecution.  Identity documents can themselves expose a holder. New military identity cards have listed the exemption subsection applying to gay men and transgender individuals, who are classified as having mental disorders; 6Rang warned that this disclosure identifies them and puts them at risk of violence and discrimination.  State pressure operates in public space as well as in paperwork. Tehran authorities publicly warned transgender people to avoid busy areas, an official advisory restricting trans visibility, and the 2017 US State Department report noted that security forces raided houses and monitored internet sites for information on LGBTI persons.  Custodial violence against trans detainees is documented. Ghazal Marzban, an imprisoned trans rights activist, recounted rape in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility in an open letter published by HRANA.  Raids on private gatherings produce mass arrests and threats of execution. An IRGC raid on a private party in Isfahan Province on 13 April 2017 involved agents reportedly firing weapons and electric Tasers; those arrested were taken to Dastgerd Prison in Isfahan, where they were led into the prison yard and told they would be executed. In February 2008 police in Isfahan raided a party and arrested 30 men, held indefinitely without a lawyer on suspicion of homosexual activity, and in January 2008 Hamzeh Chavi (18) and Loghman Hamzehpour (19) were arrested in Sardasht on sodomy and mohārebe charges.  Judicial outcomes remain lethal. Two youths were reportedly hanged in north-eastern Iran in 2006 for "sex crimes"; in 2022 two gay men in Maragheh received death sentences for "sodomy by force", a charge stemming from an accusation by a 16-year-old boy, later commuted to life in prison. The death penalty is legal from 18 for adults and from 15 for murder, and the 2017 US State Department report raised concerns about LGBTI minors. In May 2021 Ali Monfared, aged 20, was murdered allegedly by relatives.  6Rang documented forced anal or sodomy tests and degrading treatment of persons charged with homosexual conduct, part of the evidentiary practice attached to these prosecutions.  The medical regime is coercive as well as permissive. The state funds gender-reassignment surgery while placing pressure on Iranian trans people to conform to a binary transition or face legal penalty; surgery is invasive and often sub-standard and is framed publicly as protection. Two 2024–2025 media investigations describe foreign patients travelling for the same subsidised procedures while local transitions are effectively forced.  There is no same-sex marriage or civil union recognition and no legislation addressing discrimination or bias-motivated violence on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The government does not allow any political party or organisation to endorse LGBTQ rights, leaving that role to exiled groups.  Displacement is systematic rather than incidental. A 6Rang submission to the UN Independent Expert on SOGI (February 2025), "They See Us as Criminals", surveyed 25 LGBTIQ+ people who fled Iran, 96% of them from ethnic minorities, documenting the persecution driving departure; a further 6Rang submission to Iran's Universal Periodic Review at the 48th session (January–February 2025) catalogued human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people.

name: Israel
summary_text: Israel does not criminalise consensual same-sex acts, and its statutory framework combines anti-discrimination protections with publicly funded transition healthcare. Legal gender recognition has run through the courts: sex reassignment was first legally recognised in 1986, and on 27 July 2025 the High Court of Justice blocked a fast-track attempt to reverse a gender change, holding that the 2021 certificate "remains valid." As of 2025, registration of a person's previous name has been abolished for transgender people, removing the old-name traceability that previously followed a document change.  Border screening is the sharpest visitor-specific exposure. A first-person account published by Haaretz on 3 May 2023 documents a transgender traveller subjected to gender-identity humiliation at an Israeli airport, with security personnel insisting "if you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male." Later that month the Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing the searching of transgender people, a protocol change issued after complaints about humiliating searches of trans detainees and travellers.  Violence against LGBT people rose during 2025 according to official data cited by the Jerusalem Post, and Ynet reported anti-LGBTQ violence reaching a record high, with organised ambushes in which victims were lured through dating apps. Haaretz reported in February 2025 that inflammatory rhetoric from the United States was feeding into the local climate, with trans Israelis describing heightened fear.  Custody is the weakest point in the protection machinery. A law-journal study records that the state response to transgender prisoners' vulnerability has been isolation and segregation, keeping trans inmates apart from the general prison population rather than housing them in facilities matching their gender identity. An October 2019 precedent-setting case cut the other way: after a petition by ACRI, an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and move her from a male prison to a female one. She was initially held in a separate wing of the women's prison, and ACRI prepared a further petition seeking her placement with the general population.  Recognition of partners has advanced through the courts and by executive instruction. In December 2004 the Tel Aviv District Court ruled that the government had acted illegally in trying to deport the Colombian partner of a gay Israeli soldier, extending a 1999 Supreme Court rule barring deportation of foreign nationals married to Israeli citizens to common-law and same-sex couples. In March 2008 the Interior Ministry granted residency to a gay Palestinian man from Jenin to live with his partner of eight years in Tel Aviv, citing danger to his life. In December 2016 Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit instructed the Interior Ministry to extend the same citizenship rights to same-sex couples as to opposite-sex couples, replacing a prior position under which same-sex spouses waited up to seven years and typically received only permanent residency.  On 14 February 2022 Health Minister Nitzan Horowitz issued an executive directive banning licensed medical professionals, including psychologists, social workers and Ministry of Health-licensed therapists, from conducting conversion therapy. The directive does not bind rabbis, clergy or alternative practitioners and has not been codified into law by the Knesset; the governing coalition defeated a bill to ban conversion therapy on 24 February 2016 and, the same day, defeated a bill to train health professionals on gender and sexual orientation issues.  Family formation remains restricted in part. A July 2018 surrogacy law excluded single men and same-sex couples; the High Court of Justice ruled on 27 February 2020 and the Supreme Court unanimously on 11 July 2021 that the ban violated equality and the right to parenthood, effective 12 January 2022. Between 2008 and 2017 only 3 of 550 same-sex couples seeking to adopt succeeded, against more than a thousand heterosexual couples, until the government reversed course in August 2017 under Supreme Court pressure, and the Knesset voted in July 2018 to keep single men and same-sex couples out of surrogacy.  Same-sex marriage is not legislated: a Channel 10 survey reported by the Times of Israel found majority public support for it while half of MKs declined to state a position, including a culture minister who has marched in the Pride parade.  Public expression has expanded alongside sustained violence. Israel's first LGBT pride march was held on 17 September 1977, Tel Aviv's first Pride parade followed in 1993 and Eilat Pride began in 2001. Jerusalem Pride was initially banned by municipal order until a court overturned the ban; the 2005 march was attacked by Yishai Schlissel, who stabbed three people and received a ten-year sentence, and after his 2015 release he stabbed six marchers, killing teenage girl Shira Banki. On 1 August 2009 an armed attacker killed two people and injured 15 at a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv. The 2018 Aguda-organized LGBTQ strike drew over 100,000 to a Tel Aviv rally, and an estimated 250,000 marched in Tel Aviv Pride in June 2022. The 2025 Tel Aviv Pride, scheduled for 13 June, was cancelled by the municipality after Israeli strikes on Iranian targets; in 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality raised the Pride flag for the first time along the route from Sacher Park to the Knesset.  Tel Aviv functions as a regional queer hub, and Israel is widely regarded as the most progressive destination in its part of the world for trans visitors, supported by community infrastructure that includes the Municipal LGBT Community Center opened in 2008 and the Jerusalem Open House.

sources.title: Attorney General Directive 1953, Supreme Court ruling 1963, and 1988 Knesset repeal of sodomy ban
sources.documents: Decriminalization of consensual same-sex sexual activity; age of consent 16 for homosexual and heterosexual acts
sources.detail: Inherited Buggery Act 1533; 1953 directive by Attorney General Haim Cohn to refrain from enforcement; 1963 Supreme Court ruling not to apply law to consenting adults in private; formal repeal by Knesset in 1988 by omitting from criminal code. No URL visible in text.

Tel Aviv functions as a regional queer hub, and Israel is widely regarded as the most progressive destination in its part of the world for trans visitors, supported by community infrastructure that includes the Municipal LGBT Community Center opened in 2008 and the Jerusalem Open House.

name: Israel
summary_text: Israel does not criminalise consensual same-sex acts, and its statutory framework combines anti-discrimination protections with publicly funded transition healthcare. Legal gender recognition has run through the courts: sex reassignment was first legally recognised in 1986, and on 27 July 2025 the High Court of Justice blocked a fast-track attempt to reverse a gender change, holding that the 2021 certificate "remains valid." As of 2025, registration of a person's previous name has been abolished for transgender people, removing the old-name traceability that previously followed a document change.  Border screening is the sharpest visitor-specific exposure. A first-person account published by Haaretz on 3 May 2023 documents a transgender traveller subjected to gender-identity humiliation at an Israeli airport, with security personnel insisting "if you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male." Later that month the Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing the searching of transgender people, a protocol change issued after complaints about humiliating searches of trans detainees and travellers.  Violence against LGBT people rose during 2025 according to official data cited by the Jerusalem Post, and Ynet reported anti-LGBTQ violence reaching a record high, with organised ambushes in which victims were lured through dating apps. Haaretz reported in February 2025 that inflammatory rhetoric from the United States was feeding into the local climate, with trans Israelis describing heightened fear.  Custody is the weakest point in the protection machinery. A law-journal study records that the state response to transgender prisoners' vulnerability has been isolation and segregation, keeping trans inmates apart from the general prison population rather than housing them in facilities matching their gender identity. An October 2019 precedent-setting case cut the other way: after a petition by ACRI, an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and move her from a male prison to a female one. She was initially held in a separate wing of the women's prison, and ACRI prepared a further petition seeking her placement with the general population.  Recognition of partners has advanced through the courts and by executive instruction. In December 2004 the Tel Aviv District Court ruled that the government had acted illegally in trying to deport the Colombian partner of a gay Israeli soldier, extending a 1999 Supreme Court rule barring deportation of foreign nationals married to Israeli citizens to common-law and same-sex couples. In March 2008 the Interior Ministry granted residency to a gay Palestinian man from Jenin to live with his partner of eight years in Tel Aviv, citing danger to his life. In December 2016 Attorney General Avichai Mandelblit instructed the Interior Ministry to extend the same citizenship rights to same-sex couples as to opposite-sex couples, replacing a prior position under which same-sex spouses waited up to seven years and typically received only permanent residency.  On 14 February 2022 Health Minister Nitzan Horowitz issued an executive directive banning licensed medical professionals, including psychologists, social workers and Ministry of Health-licensed therapists, from conducting conversion therapy. The directive does not bind rabbis, clergy or alternative practitioners and has not been codified into law by the Knesset; the governing coalition defeated a bill to ban conversion therapy on 24 February 2016 and, the same day, defeated a bill to train health professionals on gender and sexual orientation issues.  Family formation remains restricted in part. A July 2018 surrogacy law excluded single men and same-sex couples; the High Court of Justice ruled on 27 February 2020 and the Supreme Court unanimously on 11 July 2021 that the ban violated equality and the right to parenthood, effective 12 January 2022. Between 2008 and 2017 only 3 of 550 same-sex couples seeking to adopt succeeded, against more than a thousand heterosexual couples, until the government reversed course in August 2017 under Supreme Court pressure, and the Knesset voted in July 2018 to keep single men and same-sex couples out of surrogacy.  Same-sex marriage is not legislated: a Channel 10 survey reported by the Times of Israel found majority public support for it while half of MKs declined to state a position, including a culture minister who has marched in the Pride parade.  Public expression has expanded alongside sustained violence. Israel's first LGBT pride march was held on 17 September 1977, Tel Aviv's first Pride parade followed in 1993 and Eilat Pride began in 2001. Jerusalem Pride was initially banned by municipal order until a court overturned the ban; the 2005 march was attacked by Yishai Schlissel, who stabbed three people and received a ten-year sentence, and after his 2015 release he stabbed six marchers, killing teenage girl Shira Banki. On 1 August 2009 an armed attacker killed two people and injured 15 at a lesbian and gay centre in Tel Aviv. The 2018 Aguda-organized LGBTQ strike drew over 100,000 to a Tel Aviv rally, and an estimated 250,000 marched in Tel Aviv Pride in June 2022. The 2025 Tel Aviv Pride, scheduled for 13 June, was cancelled by the municipality after Israeli strikes on Iranian targets; in 2026 the Jerusalem Municipality raised the Pride flag for the first time along the route from Sacher Park to the Knesset.  Tel Aviv functions as a regional queer hub, and Israel is widely regarded as the most progressive destination in its part of the world for trans visitors, supported by community infrastructure that includes the Municipal LGBT Community Center opened in 2008 and the Jerusalem Open House.
